anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data model and indexing choices do not align with workload access patterns, forcing otherwise well-written queries into inherently inefficient access paths.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The optimizer relies on stale, missing, or biased statistics, causing systematic cardinality errors that mislead plan generation.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage layer cannot sustain the read/write demands placed on it, leading to persistent I/O saturation and elevated latency.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a compounded symptom set: queries that already use sub-optimal access paths (full scans, non-covering index probes, excessive lookups) are paired with plans produced from wildly inaccurate row-count estimates, often selecting even more I/O-intensive strategies such as hash joins, broad parallel scans, or redundant bitmap probes. The resulting flood of random and large-volume I/O pushes the storage subsystem beyond its throughput and IOPS limits, driving queue depths high, inflating wait events (buffer reads, write-log flushes, temp-spill I/O), and creating long tail latencies perceived by both OLTP and analytical sessions. Performance becomes highly unstable: small data changes or plan recompiles can swing execution times from seconds to minutes, batch windows overrun, while foreground transactions experience intermittent stalls despite moderate CPU utilization.

Causally, a poor physical design forms the groundwork for heavy data movement; stale or missing statistics then misinform the optimizer, selecting plans that magnify the design inefficiencies; the amplified physical I/O finally collides with a saturated storage layer, turning what would have been tolerable inefficiency into a critical bottleneck. The feedback loop intensifies: slow I/O lengthens maintenance windows, delaying statistics refreshes; delayed refreshes perpetuate bad plans; prolonged write activity aggravates storage saturation. Together, these factors reinforce each other, degrading overall throughput, increasing lock durations, and eroding service-level objectives far more severely than any single anomaly alone.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time after which a TCP keepalive message that has not been acknowledged by the client should be retransmitted.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP keepalive probe is not acknowledged for tcp_keepalives_interval on systems supporting TCP_KEEPINTVL or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Controls retry timing for keepalive probes used to detect unresponsive client connections.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
